decks.title: CEL: The Companies Act, 2013
decks.description: Recall cards for CMA Final Paper 13, Chapter 1: incorporation, finance, accounts, audit, directors, meetings, investigation, mergers and minority protection.

fields.definition_md: A company whose articles (i) restrict transfer of its shares, (ii) cap membership at 200 (a One Person Company is exempt from the cap) and (iii) bar any invitation to the public to subscribe to its securities, and which meets the prescribed minimum paid-up capital.

fields.prompt_md: Counting towards the 200-member cap of a private company: who is left out and how are joint holders treated?
fields.answer_md: Joint holders of the same shares are counted as one member. Current employees who hold shares, and former employees who became members while employed and stayed on after leaving, are not counted at all.

fields.prompt_md: A private company has 150 ordinary members, 20 employee-shareholders, 10 ex-employees who took shares while employed, and 12 married couples each holding jointly. How many members count against the 200 cap?
fields.answer_md: 162. Employees and ex-employee members are ignored, and each joint-holding couple counts once: 150 + 12 = 162, so the cap is not breached.

fields.definition_md: A company that is not a private company and has the prescribed minimum paid-up capital. A subsidiary of a public company is treated as public even if its own articles keep the private-company restrictions.

fields.text_md: Minimum persons needed to form a company: public {{c1::7}}, private {{c2::2}}, One Person Company {{c3::1}}. A private company whose membership stays below the minimum for over {{c4::six months}} leaves each member severally liable for its debts incurred in that period.

fields.definition_md: A body corporate is a subsidiary of another if the other controls the composition of its board, or controls more than half of its total voting power (alone or with its own subsidiaries). Board control alone is enough: a 35% shareholder that appoints and removes most directors still makes it a subsidiary.

A company over which another company has significant influence without it being a subsidiary; a joint venture company is included. Significant influence means control of at least 20% or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement.
A company in which the Central Government, one or more State Governments, or both together hold at least 51% of paid-up capital. Subsidiaries of such a company are also Government companies.

A company or body corporate incorporated outside India that has a place of business in India (itself or through an agent, physically or electronically) and carries on business activity in India. A foreign-incorporated company that does all its business abroad is not a foreign company for the Act.

fields.reference: One Person Company: who and how (s 2(62), s 3, Incorporation Rules)
fields.prompt_md: What are the key conditions for forming and running a One Person Company?
fields.gist_md: Only a natural person can be the sole member. The memorandum names a nominee who steps in on the member's death or incapacity, and the nominee's prior written consent is filed with the Registrar. One person cannot hold more than one OPC or be nominee in more than one. A minor cannot be member or nominee. An OPC cannot be a Section 8 company and cannot do non-banking financial investment business.
fields.exceptions_md: Changing the nominee is done by notice to the company, which tells the Registrar. This is not an alteration of the memorandum.

fields.prompt_md: What are the registered-office rules on timing and on moving it within the same place or district?
fields.gist_md: The company must have a registered office from the 15th day of incorporation and verify it to the Registrar within 30 days (Form INC-22). A shift inside the same city, town or village needs only a notice to the Registrar within 15 days, with no special resolution. A shift outside the local limits of the city or town requires a special resolution.
fields.exceptions_md: Default: penalty of ₹1,000 per day, capped at ₹1 lakh, on company and each officer in default.

fields.reference: Shift between Registrar jurisdictions in one State (s 12)
fields.prompt_md: Who confirms a registered-office move from one Registrar's jurisdiction to another within the same State, and what is the timeline?
fields.gist_md: The Regional Director confirms it on the company's application and communicates within 30 days. The company files the confirmation with the Registrar within 60 days, and the Registrar of the new jurisdiction certifies within 30 days of filing. The certificate is conclusive evidence that the formalities were met and the change takes effect from its date.

fields.reference: Shift of registered office to another State (s 13)
fields.prompt_md: What approvals does shifting the registered office from one State to another need?
fields.gist_md: A special resolution altering the memorandum and the written approval of the Central Government, which should dispose of the application within 60 days after being satisfied that creditors, debenture-holders and others concerned have consented or have been provided for. Certified copies of the order are filed with the Registrars of both States, and the new State's Registrar issues a fresh certificate of incorporation. Nothing takes effect until registered.

fields.text_md: Change of company name needs the {{c1::Central Government's}} written approval, except where the only change is adding or dropping {{c2::the word 'Private'}} on conversion between company classes. Name change is not allowed for a company that has defaulted in filing {{c3::annual returns or financial statements}} or in repaying matured {{c4::deposits or debentures}}.

fields.reference: Change of objects after a public issue (s 13)
fields.prompt_md: A company still holds unspent prospectus money. How can it change its objects?
fields.gist_md: By a special resolution passed through postal ballot. The resolution details and justification must be advertised in a vernacular and an English newspaper and put on the company website, and dissenting shareholders must be offered an exit by the promoters or controlling shareholders under SEBI's rules.

fields.text_md: The memorandum must state: the {{c1::name}}, the {{c2::State}} of the registered office, the {{c3::objects}}, the members' {{c4::liability}}, the share {{c5::capital}} (if any), and for an OPC the {{c6::nominee}}.

A reserved company name is held for {{c1::20 days}} for a new company and {{c2::60 days}} for an existing company changing its name. If the name was obtained by false information, an unincorporated applicant is penalised up to {{c3::₹1 lakh}}; an incorporated company may be told to change the name within {{c4::3 months}}.

fields.prompt_md: What is an entrenchment provision in the articles and how is it inserted?
fields.gist_md: It makes specified articles changeable only under conditions tougher than a special resolution. It may be written in at formation, or added later by unanimous agreement of all members in a private company, or by special resolution in a public company. The Registrar must be notified in the prescribed form.

fields.prompt_md: How does a public company become private, and when does the change take effect?
fields.answer_md: A special resolution alters the articles to bring in the s 2(68) restrictions. The change takes effect only after the prescribed approval is obtained, and the altered articles with a copy of the approval order are filed with the Registrar within 15 days.

fields.prompt_md: What qualifies a company for a Section 8 licence and how does it differ from an ordinary company?
fields.gist_md: Its objects must lie in fields such as commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity or environmental protection, or something similar. It uses profits only for those objects and pays members no dividend. The Central Government grants the licence, the name omits 'Limited' or 'Private Limited', and the memorandum and articles cannot be changed without the Central Government's prior approval.
fields.exceptions_md: A mere intention to earn only marginal profit does not make a company non-profit; objects and the prohibition on dividends decide it.

fields.reference: Section 8: licence process and consequences (s 8, Forms INC-12/13/14)
fields.prompt_md: What is the procedure to obtain a Section 8 licence, and what follows a breach?
fields.gist_md: Apply in Form INC-12 with the memorandum (INC-13) and a professional's declaration (INC-14), plus estimated income and expenditure for the next three years. An existing company can convert by the same route with its financial statements and audit reports. The Central Government can revoke the licence for fraud or conduct against the objects, then order a name change, winding up, or amalgamation with another Section 8 company. Default is punished with ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore on the company and ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh on officers.
fields.exceptions_md: A Section 8 company can amalgamate only with another Section 8 company having similar objects.

fields.prompt_md: When must an association or partnership with many members register as a company, and who is exempt?
fields.answer_md: Under s 464 a business association or partnership with more than 50 persons (the limit set by Rule 10 of the Miscellaneous Rules) must register as a company or be formed under another law. A Hindu undivided family and professional partnerships governed by a special Act are exempt.

fields.prompt_md: Between whom does the registered constitution create contractual obligations?
fields.gist_md: It binds the company and every member as though each had signed it, and money payable by a member under it is a debt to the company. It operates between the company and each member, and between members themselves. It creates no contract between the company and an outsider, though an outsider may rely on the company having completed its internal formalities.

fields.held_md: The articles operate as a contract not only between a member and the company but also between each member and every other member.

fields.prompt_md: What does the doctrine of ultra vires say about acts beyond the memorandum, and can members ratify them?
fields.answer_md: A company has no power to act outside its memorandum's objects. An action by the board that merely exceeds its own authority within the objects can be ratified, but an act outside the company's objects is void and cannot be ratified even if every member agrees. The objects can only be widened by formally altering the memorandum.

fields.prompt_md: What must a newly incorporated company with share capital do before starting business or borrowing?
fields.gist_md: A director must file Form INC-20A within 180 days of incorporation, verified by a practising CS, CA or cost accountant, declaring that every subscriber has paid for the shares agreed to be taken. The registered office verification (INC-22) must also have been filed. Default attracts a penalty of ₹50,000 on the company and ₹1,000 a day on each officer up to ₹1 lakh, and the Registrar may start strike-off if no business is being carried on.

fields.prompt_md: A person deals with a company in a way that conflicts with its articles. What is the legal position, and is there any exception?
fields.answer_md: Memorandum and articles are public documents (s 399), so everyone dealing with the company is taken to know them (constructive notice) and acts against them at his own risk. The exception is the doctrine of indoor management: he may assume that the company's internal procedures were complied with, unless he knew of the irregularity or could easily have found it.

fields.held_md: An outsider dealing in good faith with a company may presume that the internal resolutions needed for the transaction were duly passed. The company cannot escape a bond by pointing to a missing resolution.
fields.facts_md: Directors gave a bond to a creditor. The articles allowed this only under a resolution of the company, but no such resolution had been passed.

fields.prompt_md: When can an outsider NOT rely on the indoor management rule?
fields.answer_md: When he had actual knowledge of the irregularity, or when the circumstances were suspicious enough to demand inquiry, or when the matter was something he could reasonably have found out from the public documents himself. The rule protects only those who acted in good faith on what appeared regular.

fields.held_md: A properly incorporated company is a separate legal person from its members, even if one person owns virtually all the shares and controls it.

fields.case_name: Bacha F. Guzdar v. Commissioner of Income Tax
fields.held_md: A shareholder does not own the company's assets. The property is vested in the company and a shareholder owns only his shares.

fields.prompt_md: Name a few situations in which courts lift the corporate veil.
fields.answer_md: Fraud or improper conduct, using the company as a device to avoid legal obligations or welfare laws, tax evasion where control is in issue, trading with the enemy (test of control), exchange-control violations, and cases against public policy.

fields.prompt_md: If a company has no common seal, who authorises a document that would have been sealed?
fields.answer_md: Since the 2015 amendment the common seal is optional. Without one, two directors, or a director and the company secretary where one is appointed, authorise the document.

fields.reference: Loans, guarantees, security and acquisitions: the ceiling (s 186)
fields.prompt_md: When does a company need a special resolution before lending, guaranteeing, giving security or buying securities of other bodies corporate?
fields.gist_md: When the total (existing plus proposed) would exceed the higher of two limits: 60% of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium together, or 100% of free reserves and securities premium alone. Beyond that, prior approval by special resolution at a general meeting is needed. Revaluation reserve is not a free reserve and stays out of the base.
fields.exceptions_md: A holding company's loans, guarantees and investments in its wholly owned subsidiary or joint venture company are outside this ceiling.

fields.name: Section 186 ceiling for loans, guarantees and investments
fields.variables_md: PUC = paid-up share capital; FR = free reserves; SP = securities premium account. Revaluation reserve is not part of FR.
fields.when_md: Compare against existing plus proposed loans, guarantees, security and investments. Above the limit a special resolution is needed.

fields.prompt_md: What is the minimum interest rate at which a company may lend under s 186?
fields.answer_md: It may not charge less than the prevailing yield of the Government security (1, 3, 5 or 10 year) whose maturity is closest to the tenor of the loan. A 40-month loan is therefore benchmarked to the 3-year yield, not the 1-year yield.

fields.reference: Other conditions on loans and investments (s 186)
fields.prompt_md: Besides the ceiling and rate, what procedural conditions apply to loans, investments, guarantees and security?
fields.gist_md: The sanctioning resolution must be passed at a board meeting with the consent of all directors present, and the prior approval of a public financial institution is needed if a term loan from it is outstanding (unless limits are within bounds and there is no default). A company in default on deposits or interest on them cannot lend, guarantee or acquire until it cures the default. Details go in the financial statements and in a register kept at the registered office and open to members. Investment companies may use no more than two layers of investment subsidiaries.
fields.exceptions_md: Not applicable to loans, guarantees or security by banking, insurance and housing finance companies in ordinary business, or by companies financing industrial units or infrastructure. Several investment categories (rights issues, NBFCs, investment companies) are also excluded.

fields.prompt_md: What is the penalty for contravening s 186?
fields.answer_md: Company: fine of ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh. Each officer in default: up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine of ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

fields.reference: Investments held in the company's own name (s 187)
fields.prompt_md: Must a company hold its investments in its own name, and are there exceptions?
fields.gist_md: Yes, all investments in property, securities or other assets must be made and held in the company's own name. Permitted exceptions: shares in a subsidiary may be held through nominees so that the subsidiary does not fall below its statutory minimum number of members; securities may be deposited with a bank for collecting dividend or interest, or with SBI or a scheduled bank to facilitate transfer; they may be handed over as security for a loan; and securities held as beneficial owner may stand in a depository's name.
fields.exceptions_md: If securities are not in its own name, the company keeps a register open free of charge to members and debenture-holders during business hours.

fields.reference: Deposits from the public and from members (s 73)
fields.prompt_md: On what conditions may a company accept deposits from its members?
fields.gist_md: General rule: no deposits from the public except under Chapter V. A company may take deposits from members if a general-meeting resolution authorises it and it (1) sends members a circular with its financial position, credit rating and depositor details, (2) files the circular with the Registrar 30 days before issue, (3) puts at least 20% of deposits maturing in the next financial year into a separate deposit repayment reserve account with a scheduled bank by 30 April, (4) certifies no default in deposits or interest, or that a default was cured and five years have passed, and (5) provides security if any, otherwise calls the deposits unsecured.
fields.exceptions_md: Banking companies, NBFCs and other companies notified by the Central Government after consulting the RBI are outside this section.

fields.prompt_md: A depositor's deposit falls due and the company does not pay. What can the depositor do?
fields.answer_md: Apply to the Tribunal for an order directing payment of the principal and interest, and compensation for any loss caused by non-payment. The deposit repayment reserve account cannot be used for anything but repaying deposits.

fields.text_md: Under the Deposit Rules, deposits must be repayable no earlier than {{c1::6 months}} and no later than {{c2::36 months}}. Shorter deposits are allowed up to {{c3::10%}} of paid-up capital and free reserves, and then cannot be repayable before {{c4::3 months}}.

A company that is not an eligible company can hold outstanding member deposits (with other deposits) only up to {{c1::35%}} of paid-up capital, reserves and securities premium. An eligible company is limited to {{c2::10%}} from members and {{c3::25%}} from others.

fields.prompt_md: Which company may invite deposits from the public, and what extra conditions apply?
fields.gist_md: A public company meeting the prescribed size (net worth of ₹100 crore or turnover of ₹500 crore) that has passed a special resolution. It must obtain a credit rating from a recognised agency every year during the deposit tenure and publicise it, and where deposits are secured it must create a charge on its assets within 30 days of acceptance. It may take deposits only from persons other than members under this section.

fields.text_md: The deposit repayment reserve must be funded by {{c1::30 April}} each year and cannot fall below {{c2::15%}} of deposits maturing until the end of the current and next financial year; it may be used only to {{c3::repay deposits}}.

fields.prompt_md: What penalties apply if a company accepts or fails to repay deposits in breach of s 73 or s 76?
fields.gist_md: The company pays the deposit and interest and is fined at least ₹1 crore or twice the deposit amount, whichever is lower. An officer in default faces up to seven years' imprisonment and a fine of ₹25 lakh to ₹2 crore. Knowing or intentional wrongdoing to deceive attracts the fraud provision, s 447. Officers responsible for deposits taken with fraudulent intent are personally liable for depositors' losses under s 75.

fields.prompt_md: What does the deposit register record and how long is it kept?
fields.answer_md: For each depositor: name, address and PAN, nominee, receipt number, amount, dates, tenure, interest rate and due dates, tax-deduction mandate, insurance and security details. Entries are made within seven days of the receipt and the register is kept for at least eight years after the last entry.

fields.prompt_md: Who can and cannot be a trustee for depositors in a secured deposit scheme?
fields.answer_md: A trustee is appointed before the circular is issued and the trust deed (Form DPT-2) must be executed at least 7 days before the circular. A director, KMP, employee, depositor, a person indebted to the company or its group, a guarantor of the deposits, or anyone with a material financial link or related to those persons cannot act.

fields.definition_md: Debenture stock, bonds or any other instrument of a company that acknowledges a debt, whether or not it creates a charge on the company's assets.

fields.reference: 2026 revision: Form CRL-1 on layers of subsidiaries
fields.prompt_md: What changed in the filing on the number of layers of subsidiaries?
fields.gist_md: The Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Amendment Rules, 2025 (notified 27 June 2025, effective 14 July 2025) replaced the earlier Form CRL-1 with a revised electronic Form CRL-1, simplifying disclosure of holding and subsidiary structures and making layered group structures clearer.

fields.prompt_md: Out of what funds may a company declare or pay a dividend?
fields.gist_md: Only from (a) the current year's profit after providing for depreciation, (b) profits of earlier years that remain undistributed, again after depreciation, or (c) both. Unrealised or notional gains, asset revaluation and fair-value changes are excluded when computing the profit. Dividends cannot come from reserves that are not free reserves. Past losses and accumulated depreciation are set off first, and a company in default on deposits cannot declare a dividend. Transfer to reserves before declaring a dividend is at the company's discretion.
fields.exceptions_md: The default bar on deposits does not apply to a Government company wholly owned by the Centre and/or States.

fields.text_md: Dividend out of free reserves when current profits are inadequate: the rate cannot exceed the {{c1::average of the last three years' rates}}; the draw cannot exceed {{c2::one-tenth}} of paid-up capital plus free reserves; the draw first {{c3::sets off the year's losses}}; and reserves left must not fall below {{c4::15%}} of paid-up capital.

fields.prompt_md: How soon after declaring a dividend must the money be set aside, and where?
fields.gist_md: Within 5 days of the declaration, the whole dividend (interim dividends too) must be deposited in a separate account with a scheduled bank. Any default can attract the penalty under s 127.
fields.exceptions_md: Not applicable to a Government company whose entire paid-up capital is held by the Central and/or State Governments.

fields.prompt_md: Who declares an interim dividend, what limits apply, and what happens to it at the AGM?
fields.gist_md: The board may declare it at any time in the year or between year-end and the AGM, out of surplus in the profit and loss account or current profits up to the quarter before declaration. If the company has made a loss in the year up to the preceding quarter, the rate cannot be above the average of the previous three years' rates. An interim dividend is confirmed at the AGM and is treated with the final dividend. A final dividend is declared at the AGM on the board's recommendation, and once declared cannot be revoked.

fields.prompt_md: To whom is a dividend payable, and in what form?
fields.answer_md: Only to the registered holder of the share, to his order, or to his banker. It is paid in cash, by cheque, warrant or electronic mode. Issue of bonus shares by capitalising reserves is a different matter and is not a dividend payment.

fields.prompt_md: What are the consequences if a declared dividend is not paid in time, and when is there no offence?
fields.gist_md: Every director knowingly party to the default faces up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of at least ₹1,000 per day of default. The company owes simple interest at 18% per annum for the period of default. No offence arises if payment was prevented by law, if the shareholder's payment instructions could not be followed and he was told so, if there is a dispute over the right to the dividend, if the dividend was lawfully set off against sums the shareholder owes, or if the failure was not the company's fault.
fields.exceptions_md: Silence is the trap: a bounced bank credit that the company never tells the shareholder about is not within the exception.

fields.reference: Unpaid dividend and the Investor Education and Protection Fund (s 124, s 125)
fields.prompt_md: What happens to dividend that remains unclaimed?
fields.gist_md: It sits in the unpaid dividend account. If it stays unclaimed for seven years from transfer to that account, the company must remit it with accrued interest to the IEPF within 90 days of it becoming due. The company keeps a record of the persons entitled for 8 years after transfer. Other items that go to the IEPF after seven years include share application money due for refund, matured deposits and debentures and interest on them. A claimant applies to the Fund's authority for payment.

fields.prompt_md: Which listed entities must have a dividend distribution policy under SEBI LODR?
fields.answer_md: The top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation (computed at 31 March each year) must adopt and publish one on their website and in the annual report. Others may do so voluntarily. The policy covers when shareholders may expect dividends, financial and external factors, use of retained earnings, and parameters for different share classes.

fields.prompt_md: Where must books of account be kept, in what system, and for how long?
fields.gist_md: At the registered office, though the board may place all or some at another place in India if it files notice of the full address with the Registrar within 7 days. They follow the accrual basis and double entry. They must be kept in good order for at least 8 financial years, longer if an investigation is ordered. The MD, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the CFO or any person the board charges is responsible, and default draws a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh.

fields.reference: Books in electronic form (s 128, Accounts Rule 3)
fields.prompt_md: What conditions apply when books of account are kept electronically?
fields.gist_md: The records must stay accessible in India and be reproducible in a legible form, be retained in the original format or one that reproduces the information accurately, and not be altered (branch information must show what was originally received). There must be a proper storage and retrieval system. Back-ups, including of data held abroad, must be kept periodically on servers physically located in India. Each year at the time of filing financial statements the company tells the Registrar the service provider's name, IP address and location, and the cloud address if cloud-hosted.

fields.prompt_md: Who may inspect a company's books of account, and how is financial information held abroad dealt with?
fields.answer_md: Any director may inspect during business hours at the registered office or other place in India. For records kept outside India, summarised returns go to the registered office every quarter. A director who needs further offshore information must ask in person (not through an agent or attorney holder) and the company must produce it within 15 days. Inspection of a subsidiary's books needs a board resolution authorising the person.

fields.definition_md: Balance sheet, statement of profit and loss (or income and expenditure account for a not-for-profit), cash flow statement, statement of changes in equity where applicable, and explanatory notes. One Person Companies, small companies and dormant companies need not include a cash flow statement.

fields.prompt_md: When must a company prepare consolidated statements, and who can skip them?
fields.gist_md: A company with subsidiaries (associates count too) prepares consolidated statements in the same form, lays them before the AGM with its own accounts, and attaches Form AOC-1 with the subsidiaries' salient features. A company may skip them if it is a wholly owned subsidiary, or a partly owned one whose other members, intimated in writing, do not object; its securities are unlisted and not in the process of listing; and an ultimate or intermediate holding company files compliant consolidated statements with the Registrar.

fields.prompt_md: After board approval, who signs the financial statements and Board's report?
fields.gist_md: The statements are signed on behalf of the board by the chairperson if authorised, or by two directors (one the managing director and the other the CEO if he is a director), plus the CFO and the company secretary where appointed. In a One Person Company one director signs. The Board's report is signed by the chairperson if authorised, otherwise by at least two directors one of whom is the managing director, or by the sole director.

fields.prompt_md: List the statements a Directors' Responsibility Statement must contain.
fields.answer_md: That applicable accounting standards were followed with explanation of material departures; accounting policies were consistent and judgments prudent to give a true and fair view; proper accounting records were maintained to safeguard assets and detect fraud; accounts were prepared on a going-concern basis; (for listed companies) internal financial controls were laid down and operate effectively; and systems exist to ensure compliance with all applicable laws.

fields.prompt_md: Name the key contents of the Board's report beyond the state of affairs.
fields.answer_md: The annual return web address, number of board meetings, the Directors' Responsibility Statement, auditor-reported frauds not sent to the Government, the independent directors' declaration, the nomination and remuneration policy, the board's replies to auditor and secretarial auditor qualifications, loans, guarantees and investments under s 186, related-party contracts (Form AOC-2), proposed reserves and dividend, material post-balance-sheet changes, energy, technology and foreign exchange data, risk management and CSR policy, and the board evaluation statement.

fields.prompt_md: How long before the AGM must financial statements reach members and when can that be shortened?
fields.gist_md: At least 21 days before the meeting. A shorter period is treated as valid if members who are a majority in number and hold at least 95% of the voting capital agree. Listed companies satisfy the rule by keeping the documents open for inspection at the registered office for 21 days and sending a salient-features statement (Form AOC-3) unless a member asks for the full set. Sending by electronic mode is allowed for demat holders with registered email IDs.
fields.exceptions_md: For a Section 8 company the notice period is 14 days instead of 21.

fields.reference: Filing financial statements with the Registrar (s 137)
fields.prompt_md: Within what time are adopted financial statements filed?
fields.gist_md: Within 30 days of the AGM at which they were adopted. If they were not adopted, the unadopted statements are filed within 30 days of the AGM and kept as provisional. An OPC files within 180 days of year-end. If the AGM was not held, the statements and reasons are filed within 30 days of the last date by which the AGM was due. Default: company ₹10,000 plus ₹100 per day up to ₹2 lakh; the MD and CFO each ₹10,000 plus ₹100 per day up to ₹50,000.

fields.prompt_md: Which companies must appoint an internal auditor?
fields.gist_md: Every listed company; every unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more, turnover of ₹200 crore or more, bank or institution borrowings above ₹100 crore, or deposits of ₹25 crore or more in the preceding year; and every private company with turnover of ₹200 crore or more or such borrowings above ₹100 crore. The internal auditor may be a CA, cost accountant or other professional the board chooses, and may be an employee.

fields.reference: 2026 revision: Board's report disclosures (Accounts Second Amendment Rules, 2025)
fields.prompt_md: What new items must the Board's report now disclose under the 2025 amendment effective 14 July 2025?
fields.gist_md: The number of sexual-harassment complaints received, disposed of and pending for over 90 days under the POSH Act, and a statement of compliance with the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961.

fields.prompt_md: 2026 revision: what changed in how accounts are filed (MCA V3)?
fields.answer_md: Signed financial statements, Board's report extracts and auditors' reports (standalone and consolidated) must be filed only through the MCA V3 portal in PDF or XBRL mode. Older AOC filings were replaced by e-AOC-1 and e-AOC-2, with revised versions of AOC-4 (V3) and AOC-4 CFS and revised V3 formats for NBFC variants.

fields.prompt_md: 2026 revision: the Ind AS Second Amendment Rules, 2025.
fields.answer_md: Notified on 13 August 2025 to align Ind AS with updated international developments; it affects recognition, measurement and disclosure for companies that must follow Ind AS. The supplementary note gives no further detail.

fields.prompt_md: How and when is the statutory auditor appointed, and what must be filed?
fields.gist_md: At the first AGM the company appoints an individual or firm to hold office until the sixth AGM, and then every sixth AGM thereafter. Before appointment the company obtains the auditor's written consent and a certificate that the appointment meets the prescribed conditions and eligibility. The appointment (including re-appointment) is notified to the auditor and filed in Form ADT-1 within 15 days of the meeting. Where an Audit Committee exists, it recommends the appointment after weighing the auditor's qualifications, experience and any pending conduct proceedings.

fields.reference: Term limits and rotation of auditors (s 139(2)-(4), Audit Rules 5-6)
fields.prompt_md: What are the term limits for auditors and which companies are covered?
fields.gist_md: Listed companies and the prescribed classes cannot appoint an individual for more than one term of five consecutive years or a firm for more than two such terms. Covered classes: unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, private companies with ₹20 crore or more, and any company with public borrowings or deposits of ₹50 crore or more. After the term the auditor is barred from the same company for five years, as are firms with a common partner or in the same network. One Person Companies and small companies are not covered.

fields.reference: First auditor and casual vacancy: non-government company (s 139(6), (8))
fields.prompt_md: How are a first auditor and a casual vacancy filled in an ordinary company?
fields.gist_md: The board appoints the first auditor within 30 days of registration, failing which the members appoint at an EGM within 90 days; he serves until the first AGM. The board fills a casual vacancy within 30 days. If the vacancy arises from a resignation, the general meeting must approve the appointment within three months of the board's recommendation. A casual-vacancy appointee holds office until the next AGM.

fields.prompt_md: Who appoints the auditor of a government company and within what timelines?
fields.gist_md: The Comptroller and Auditor General appoints the auditor within 180 days of the start of the financial year, and the auditor serves until the AGM. For the first auditor, the CAG has 60 days from registration, the board then has 30 days, and if it fails the members appoint at an EGM within 60 days. A casual vacancy is filled by the CAG within 30 days, failing which the board fills it within the next 30 days. This covers companies controlled by Central or State Governments, not only those with 51% holding.

fields.prompt_md: What is needed to remove an auditor before the end of his term?
fields.gist_md: A special resolution and the prior approval of the Central Government, sought in Form ADT-2 within 30 days of the board's resolution. The general meeting must be held within 60 days of receiving the approval. The auditor must be given a fair chance to be heard before removal, and the special resolution is filed in MGT-14.

fields.prompt_md: What must an auditor who resigns do, and what happens if he does not?
fields.gist_md: Within 30 days of resigning, file a statement with the company and the Registrar in Form ADT-3 giving reasons (for government companies, also with the CAG). If he does not, the penalty is the lower of ₹50,000 or the amount of his remuneration, plus ₹500 for each continuing day, up to ₹2 lakh.

fields.prompt_md: A company wants a different auditor than the retiring one at the AGM before the retiring auditor has served his full term. What process is needed?
fields.answer_md: Special notice of the resolution. A copy goes at once to the retiring auditor, who may make a written representation that the company must circulate to members (or, if too late, he may require it to be read out at the meeting; if not sent, a copy goes to the Registrar).

fields.text_md: An auditor's relative may hold securities in the company only up to face value {{c1::₹1 lakh}}. The auditor is disqualified if he owes the company more than {{c2::₹5 lakh}}, has guaranteed a third party's dues to the company beyond {{c3::₹1 lakh}}, or already holds more than {{c4::20}} company audits.

fields.prompt_md: Besides financial thresholds, who else is disqualified from being auditor under s 141(3)?
fields.answer_md: A body corporate (other than an LLP), an officer or employee of the company or a partner or employee of such a person, anyone with a business relationship with the company or its group, someone whose relative is a director or KMP, a person in full-time employment elsewhere, a person convicted of fraud within the last 10 years, and one who renders prohibited s 144 services to the company or its group.

fields.prompt_md: What happens if a serving auditor becomes disqualified?
fields.answer_md: He is deemed to have vacated office and the position is a casual vacancy.

fields.prompt_md: Who fixes the statutory auditor's remuneration, and what does it include?
fields.answer_md: The company in general meeting, or as the meeting decides; the board fixes it for the first auditor. It includes out-of-pocket expenses and facilities for the audit but not pay for other services the auditor performs at the company's request.

fields.reference: Auditor's powers of access and inquiry (s 143(1))
fields.prompt_md: What can the auditor demand and inquire into?
fields.gist_md: A right of access at all times to books and vouchers wherever kept, and to information and explanations from officers. He may inquire whether secured loans are properly secured and not prejudicial, whether book-entry transactions harm the company, whether securities were sold below cost (other than by investment or banking companies), whether loans are shown as deposits, whether personal expenses are charged to revenue, and whether shares said to be allotted for cash were really paid for. A holding company's auditor can access subsidiary and associate records for consolidation.

fields.reference: Fraud reporting by auditors (s 143(12), Audit Rule 13)
fields.prompt_md: What is the procedure when an auditor suspects fraud by officers or employees?
fields.gist_md: The auditor first sends his report to the board or Audit Committee and asks for a response within 45 days. He then forwards it to the Central Government with his comments within 15 days of the reply, or with a note if no reply came in 45 days, and in every case within 60 days of acquiring knowledge. Under the 2025 revision the report goes electronically in Form ADT-4 and the earlier postal and letterhead-based submission has been discontinued. An auditor reporting in good faith is not in breach of duty.
fields.exceptions_md: Penalty for not reporting: ₹1 lakh for an unlisted company's auditor, ₹5 lakh for a listed company's. The same applies to a cost auditor or secretarial auditor.

fields.prompt_md: 2026 revision: which audit forms were revised for MCA V3 and what else changed?
fields.answer_md: ADT-1 (appointment), ADT-2 (removal), ADT-3 (resignation) and ADT-4 (fraud reporting) were revised as electronic V3 versions. Rule 13(2) was substituted so fraud reports are filed electronically in ADT-4, and postal submission and letterhead requirements were removed (Audit and Auditors Amendment Rules, 2025, effective 14 July 2025).

fields.prompt_md: Which services may a statutory auditor not render to the company or its group?
fields.answer_md: Accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, designing or implementing financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory, investment banking, outsourced financial services, management services and any other prescribed service. 'Directly or indirectly' covers services through relatives, partners, parent, subsidiary or associate entities and entities the auditor or partner influences or whose brand he uses.

fields.reference: Penalties for contravention of the audit provisions (s 147)
fields.prompt_md: What are the penalties for breach of ss 139 to 146?
fields.gist_md: Company: ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh. Officer in default: ₹10,000 to ₹1 lakh. An auditor contravening ss 139, 144 or 145: ₹25,000 to ₹5 lakh or four times his remuneration, whichever is less. If knowingly or wilfully to deceive: up to one year's imprisonment and ₹50,000 to ₹25 lakh or eight times remuneration, whichever is less. A convicted auditor must also refund his remuneration and pay damages. In a firm, partners who acted fraudulently or abetted fraud are liable jointly and severally with the firm.

fields.prompt_md: Who audits cost records and how is the cost auditor appointed?
fields.answer_md: A cost accountant in practice appointed by the board on the Audit Committee's recommended remuneration, and ratified by shareholders. The Central Government orders cost records (Form CRA-1) only for prescribed classes of companies.

fields.prompt_md: Which companies are outside CARO 2020?
fields.answer_md: Banking and insurance companies, Section 8 companies, One Person Companies, small companies, and a private company that is not a subsidiary or holding of a public company and has paid-up capital plus reserves of no more than ₹1 crore, borrowings of no more than ₹1 crore and revenue of no more than ₹10 crore.

fields.text_md: Minimum directors under s 149(1): public company {{c1::3}}, private company {{c2::2}}, One Person Company {{c3::1}}. The maximum is {{c4::15}}, which can be exceeded only by a {{c5::special resolution}}.

fields.prompt_md: Which companies must have at least one woman director, and how fast must a vacancy be filled?
fields.gist_md: Every listed company, and every other public company with paid-up capital of ₹100 crore or more or turnover of ₹300 crore or more. A newly incorporated company that falls in these classes has six months from incorporation to comply. A casual vacancy must be filled by the Board by the next Board meeting or within three months of the vacancy, whichever is later.

fields.prompt_md: What is the residency requirement for a company's board?
fields.gist_md: At least one director must have been in India for a total of 182 days or more during the year. A company incorporated between 1 April and 30 September 2014 had to appoint such a director either at incorporation or within six months after it.

fields.reference: Independent directors: how many (s 149(4), Appointment Rule 4)
fields.prompt_md: What proportion or number of independent directors must a company have?
fields.gist_md: A listed public company needs at least one-third of its directors to be independent, and any fraction is rounded up to one. Other public companies need at least two independent directors if any one of these holds: paid-up capital ₹10 crore or more, turnover ₹100 crore or more, or total loans, debentures and deposits above ₹50 crore (measured on the last audited accounts). A higher number applies if the Audit Committee composition demands it. A vacancy is to be filled by the next Board meeting or within three months, whichever is later.

fields.definition_md: A director other than a managing director, whole-time director or nominee director, who in the Board's opinion has integrity and relevant expertise and experience, and who is free of the promoter, family, pecuniary and employment ties listed in s 149(6).

fields.prompt_md: Which relationships and ties disqualify a person from being an independent director under s 149(6)?
fields.answer_md: Being or having been a promoter of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate; being related to its promoters or directors; having a pecuniary relationship beyond director's remuneration and permitted small transactions in the last two years and the current one; relatives with large holdings, debts, guarantees or transactions; in the previous three years having been a KMP or employee, or an employee, proprietor or partner of its auditor, company secretary or cost auditor firm, or of a legal or consulting firm with big business with it; holding 2% or more of voting power with relatives; or heading a non-profit that gets 25% or more of its receipts from the company group.

fields.prompt_md: How does a person qualify to be an independent director on the IICA databank, and who is exempt from the test?
fields.answer_md: He registers on the databank kept by the Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs and must pass its proficiency examination. No test is needed for those with 10 years as a KMP, 10 years as an advocate or practising CA, CMA or CS, or service at a director-equivalent government pay level in commerce, corporate, finance or industry matters.

fields.reference: Appointment of directors: basic rules (s 152(1)-(5), s 154)
fields.prompt_md: Who are the first directors, who appoints later directors, and what must a new director file?
fields.gist_md: If the articles do not name them, the individual subscribers to the memorandum are the first directors; in an OPC the sole member is the first director. Later directors are appointed by the company in general meeting unless the articles provide another method. No one can be appointed without a DIN under s 154, and each appointee furnishes his DIN and a declaration that he is not disqualified. He may not act until he consents to the office, and the consent is filed with the Registrar in Form DIR-12 within 30 days of appointment.
fields.exceptions_md: The consent requirement does not apply to a director appointed by the Central or State Government, or to a Section 8 company.

fields.reference: Retirement by rotation: how many directors (s 152(6))
fields.prompt_md: What share of directors retire by rotation and how many go at each AGM?
fields.gist_md: At least two-thirds of the total directors must be rotational, and the articles may make more or all of them so. Of those, one-third retire at every AGM, or the nearest whole number if the count is not a multiple of three. Directors appointed by the Central Government, financial institutions or banks are left out of this count. The directors who have served longest since last appointment retire first, and ties are settled by lot or agreement.

fields.text_md: A public company has 9 rotational directors. At the first AGM {{c1::3}} must retire, which is one-third. If it had 10 rotational directors, the number nearest one-third is {{c2::3}}.

fields.reference: When a retiring director's seat is not filled (s 152(7))
fields.prompt_md: What happens if the AGM does not fill the seat of a retiring director?
fields.gist_md: Unless the meeting expressly resolved not to fill it, the meeting stands adjourned to the same day next week, same time and place (or the next non-holiday if that day is a national holiday). If the seat is still not filled at the adjourned meeting, the retiring director is deemed reappointed. This does not happen if a reappointment resolution was put and lost, he gave written notice that he is unwilling, he is disqualified, a special or ordinary resolution is required by the Act for his appointment, or s 162 applies.
fields.exceptions_md: Rotation does not apply to a wholly government-owned Government company or its wholly owned subsidiary.

fields.reference: Candidature of a non-retiring person (s 160, Appointment Rule 13)
fields.prompt_md: How can an outsider stand for election as a director at a general meeting?
fields.gist_md: He, or a member proposing him, leaves a written notice at the registered office at least 14 days before the meeting, with a deposit of ₹1 lakh. The deposit is refunded if he is elected or gets more than 25% of valid votes. No deposit is needed if the Nomination and Remuneration Committee or the Board recommends him. The company must tell members at least 7 days before the meeting, by electronic mail or writing and on its website, or alternatively by advertising once in an English newspaper and once in a vernacular newspaper circulating in the registered office's district.
fields.exceptions_md: Section 160 does not apply to wholly government-owned Government companies and their wholly owned subsidiaries, private companies, or companies whose articles provide for election of directors by ballot.

fields.prompt_md: Who can appoint an additional director and for how long does he serve?
fields.gist_md: The Board, if the articles authorise it. He serves until the next AGM or the last date on which that AGM should have been held, whichever is earlier. A person who failed to win election at a general meeting cannot be brought in as an additional director.

fields.prompt_md: When can an alternate director be appointed and when must he leave?
fields.gist_md: The Board, if authorised by the articles or by a general-meeting resolution, may appoint one to act for a director who will be absent from India for at least three months. A person already acting as an alternate for another director cannot be chosen, and one acting for an independent director must himself qualify as independent. He holds office no longer than the original director could, and leaves as soon as the original returns to India. If the original's term ends before he returns, automatic reappointment applies to the original, not to the alternate.

fields.prompt_md: Who can nominate a director, and does nomination alone make him a director?
fields.gist_md: An institution under a law or an agreement (for example a lender), or the Central or State Government by virtue of its shareholding in a Government company. Nomination is not appointment: the Board must still appoint him in the proper manner subject to the articles.

fields.prompt_md: How is the seat of a director appointed in general meeting filled if he leaves early?
fields.gist_md: The Board fills it at a Board meeting, subject to the articles, and the next general meeting approves it. The new person holds office only for the unexpired term of the director he replaced.

fields.prompt_md: How is a small shareholders' director chosen, and what limits apply to him?
fields.gist_md: A listed company may have one, elected on notice from 1,000 small shareholders or one-tenth of such shareholders, whichever is lower; a small shareholder holds shares of nominal value not above ₹20,000. The candidate's notice goes in 14 days before the meeting with his DIN, no-disqualification statement and consent. He counts as independent if eligible under s 149(6), is not subject to rotation, serves up to three consecutive years without reappointment, and may hold the seat in no more than two non-competing companies. For three years after leaving he cannot be associated with that company in any capacity.
fields.exceptions_md: A listed company may choose to have such a director suo motu, in which case the 14-day notice route is not needed.

fields.prompt_md: Can the articles provide for proportional representation of directors?
fields.gist_md: Yes. The articles may fill at least two-thirds of the directors by proportional representation, through single transferable vote, cumulative voting or otherwise, with such appointments made once every three years.

fields.reference: Disqualifications for appointment as director: personal (s 164(1))
fields.prompt_md: List the grounds in s 164(1) that make a person ineligible for directorship.
fields.gist_md: Unsound mind declared by a competent court; undischarged insolvent or a pending insolvency application; conviction with at least six months' imprisonment (barred until five years after the sentence ends, and permanently barred if the sentence was seven years or more); a court or Tribunal disqualification order in force; unpaid calls on his shares six months after the due date; conviction for a related-party offence under s 188 in the last five years; no DIN; and exceeding the directorship ceiling in s 165(1).

fields.prompt_md: When is a director barred because of his company's defaults, and for how long?
fields.gist_md: If a company has not filed financial statements or annual returns for three continuous financial years, or has failed for a year or more to repay deposits, redeem debentures, pay interest, or pay a declared preference dividend, then any person who is or was a director of it cannot be reappointed there or appointed elsewhere for five years from the date of default. A person newly appointed to such a company is protected for six months.
fields.exceptions_md: Section 164(2) does not apply to a Government company.

fields.prompt_md: Does a pending appeal save a person from disqualification for conviction, a court order or a related-party offence?
fields.answer_md: Not permanently. Those three disqualifications start only after 30 days from the conviction or order, and if an appeal is filed in that period, after 7 days from its disposal (and likewise for a further appeal filed within the 7 days). A private company may add further disqualifications in its articles.

fields.prompt_md: What must be done when a director resigns, and by whom?
fields.gist_md: He gives written notice to the company, and the Board takes note of it. The company informs the Registrar in Form DIR-12 within 30 days of receiving the notice, posts it on its website if it has one, and mentions it in the directors' report for the next general meeting. The director also files a copy with reasons in Form DIR-11 within 30 days.

fields.reference: Removal of a director by members (s 169)
fields.prompt_md: How can a company remove a director before his term ends?
fields.gist_md: By ordinary resolution on special notice, after giving him a reasonable chance to be heard. On getting the notice the company sends a copy at once to the director, who may be heard at the meeting whether or not he is a member. The vacancy may be filled at the same meeting if the proposal was in the special notice, and the new director serves out the removed one's remaining term. If it is not filled then, the Board fills it as a casual vacancy, but the removed person cannot be reappointed. He keeps any right to compensation for early termination.
fields.exceptions_md: Not removable this way: a director appointed by the Tribunal under s 242 and one elected under proportional representation. A second-term independent director needs a special resolution.

fields.reference: Vacation of office by a director (s 167(1))
fields.prompt_md: On what grounds does a director's office become vacant automatically?
fields.gist_md: Incurring any s 164 disqualification (for a s 164(2) default, he vacates in all companies except the defaulting one); missing every Board meeting held in 12 months, with or without leave; breaching s 184 on interested contracts or failing to disclose his interest; court or Tribunal disqualification; conviction with at least six months' imprisonment (with the same 30 and 7-day protection as in s 164); removal under the Act; and ceasing the post in a holding, subsidiary or associate company by virtue of which he was appointed.

fields.prompt_md: A director has vacated office under s 167 but keeps acting. Another thing: all the directors have vacated. What follows in each case?
fields.answer_md: A director who knowingly functions after vacating is fined ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh. If all directors vacate, the promoter, or failing him the Central Government, appoints the required number, who serve until the company appoints directors in general meeting. A private company's articles may add other grounds for vacation.

fields.definition_md: A director entrusted with substantial powers of management by the articles, an agreement, or a resolution of the company or the Board. Routine administrative acts such as affixing the seal, signing cheques or negotiable instruments, signing share certificates or directing registration of transfers do not count as substantial powers.
A director in the whole-time employment of the company, also called an executive director. A function may be attached to the post, as with Director (Finance).

An individual who, under the Board's superintendence, control and direction, manages the whole or substantially the whole of the company's affairs, under whatever name and whether or not under a service contract.

fields.reference: Terms and eligibility for MD, WTD and manager (s 196(1)-(3))
fields.prompt_md: What limits apply to the term and the age of a managing director, whole-time director or manager?
fields.gist_md: A company cannot have a managing director and a manager at the same time. The term is at most five years at a time, and reappointment cannot be made earlier than one year before the term ends. The person must be at least 21 and under 70, though a person aged 70 or more can be appointed by special resolution. He must not be an insolvent, have suspended payment to creditors or compounded with them, or have been convicted of an offence and sentenced to more than six months.

fields.prompt_md: Beyond s 196(3), what further conditions does Schedule V set for a managerial person?
fields.answer_md: He must not have been sentenced to imprisonment, or fined more than ₹1,000, under the specified Acts, nor detained under COFEPOSA. If he is a managerial person in several companies his total pay stays within the Schedule's ceiling. He must be resident in India, which includes one who has stayed in India continuously for at least 12 months before appointment having come for employment, business or vacation.

fields.reference: Procedure for appointing an MD, WTD or manager (s 196(4)-(5))
fields.prompt_md: What steps does the appointment of a managing director, whole-time director or manager require?
fields.gist_md: The Board approves the appointment and the terms and pay at a meeting, and the next general meeting must approve them. The notice for either meeting must set out the terms, the remuneration and any director's interest. If the terms vary from Schedule V, the Central Government's approval is needed. A return in Form MR-1 goes to the Registrar within 60 days. Acts done before shareholder approval are valid even if the meeting then refuses it.

fields.reference: Key managerial personnel: who and which companies (s 203, Managerial Rule 8)
fields.prompt_md: Who are the whole-time KMP, and which companies must have them?
fields.gist_md: The managing director, or the CEO, or the manager (or if none, a whole-time director), plus the company secretary and the chief financial officer. Every listed company, and every other public company with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, must have them. They are appointed by Board resolution stating the terms and pay.

fields.reference: Chairperson and MD/CEO, and multiple offices (s 203)
fields.prompt_md: Can one person be chairperson and also MD or CEO, and can a KMP hold office in more than one company?
fields.gist_md: Not together, unless the articles provide otherwise or the company does not carry on multiple businesses (the rule also does not bind notified multi-business companies with a CEO for each business). A whole-time KMP may hold office in only one company at a time, except in its subsidiary, though he can be a director elsewhere with the Board's permission. A person who is MD or manager of one company may be appointed MD of one other, by a unanimous Board resolution of the directors present with specific notice to all directors then in India.

fields.prompt_md: How long does the Board have to fill a vacancy in a whole-time KMP post?
fields.answer_md: Six months from the date the post fell vacant, at a Board meeting.

fields.prompt_md: What is the maximum remuneration payable to directors and managers as a percentage of net profit?
fields.gist_md: For all directors including MD, WTD and manager of a public company together: 11% of net profit. Within that: a single MD, WTD or manager 5%; more than one such, 10% in total; directors who are neither MD nor WTD 1% if there is an MD or WTD, and 3% if there is none. Exceeding these needs the company's approval in general meeting, subject to Schedule V and, for the individual sub-limits, a special resolution. Net profit is computed under s 198 but without deducting directors' remuneration.

fields.text_md: Overall managerial pay cap is {{c1::11%}} of net profits; one MD, WTD or manager {{c2::5%}}; more than one such {{c3::10%}} together; non-executive directors {{c4::1%}} with an MD or WTD, {{c5::3%}} without.

fields.reference: Remuneration and the director's other services (s 197(4)-(6))
fields.prompt_md: How is a director's remuneration fixed, and is it inclusive of pay for other roles?
fields.gist_md: It is fixed by the articles, an ordinary resolution or, if the articles require, a special resolution. It includes pay for services in any other capacity, except professional services where the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (or the Board, if there is no such committee) is satisfied that the director has the qualification to practise. It may be monthly, a percentage of net profit, or both. Premium for fidelity-guarantee insurance against misfeasance is not remuneration.

fields.prompt_md: What limits apply to sitting fees paid to directors?
fields.gist_md: The Board decides them, up to ₹1 lakh per Board or committee meeting. Independent and women directors cannot be paid less than other directors. Sitting fees are over and above the percentage ceilings on remuneration.

fields.reference: Remuneration when profits are absent or inadequate (s 197(3), (11))
fields.prompt_md: What governs pay to directors when a company has no profit or inadequate profit?
fields.gist_md: Pay beyond sitting fees can be given only in line with Schedule V. If the company cannot satisfy Schedule V, it needs the Central Government's prior approval. In that case, a term in the memorandum, articles, an agreement or a resolution that increases the pay is ineffective unless it conforms.

fields.prompt_md: A director has drawn more than the permitted remuneration. What must he do?
fields.gist_md: Refund the excess to the company within two years, or any shorter period the company allows, and hold it in trust for the company until he does. The company cannot simply waive the recovery.

fields.prompt_md: What must a listed company's Board report show about pay?
fields.gist_md: The ratio of each director's remuneration to the median employee's pay, and a statement of the top 10 paid employees who earned at least ₹1.25 crore for a full year, or at least ₹8.5 lakh per month for part of a year, or who earned more than the MD, WTD or manager while holding 2% or more of the equity with spouse and dependent children. The statement gives designation, pay, qualification, experience, age, start date, last job, shareholding and any relationship to a director.

fields.prompt_md: Penalty for breaching s 197, and what must the auditor say about managerial pay?
fields.answer_md: Fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh on a person contravening the section. The auditor's s 143 report must state whether the remuneration complies with s 197 and whether any director was paid above the limit.

fields.prompt_md: Can a managing or whole-time director who draws commission from the company also take pay from its holding or subsidiary?
fields.answer_md: Yes, he is not disqualified from receiving remuneration or commission from the holding or a subsidiary company, provided the company discloses it in the Board's report.

fields.reference: Computing net profit for managerial pay (s 198)
fields.prompt_md: How are profits calculated for the s 197 ceilings?
fields.gist_md: Start from the profit and loss account. Credit is given for subsidies from governments or public authorities. Credit is not given for premium on shares or debentures, profit on forfeited shares, capital profits including sale of an undertaking, profit on sale of capital fixed assets (with a proviso allowing the part of any excess over written-down value that does not exceed original cost less written-down value), fair-value changes and unrealised or notional gains. Usual working charges, directors' pay, staff bonus, interest, repairs, depreciation under s 123, legal compensation and bad debts written off are deducted, but income tax, voluntary compensation and capital losses are not.

fields.prompt_md: What must the Central Government or the company weigh when fixing remuneration in a company with no or inadequate profit (s 200)?
fields.answer_md: The company's financial position, the person's pay in other roles and from other companies, his qualifications and experience, the last three years' financial and operating performance, the link between pay and performance, proportionality against other directors and staff, any difference between director and employee pay policy, and the securities he holds including options and pledged shares.

fields.reference: Powers of the Board and how they are exercised (s 179(1)-(2), (4))
fields.prompt_md: How wide is the Board's power, and who can restrict it?
fields.gist_md: The Board may exercise all powers the company may exercise, except those the Act reserves to the general meeting. It acts collectively, and no individual director has Board power unless authorised. A general-meeting regulation cannot invalidate an earlier valid act of the Board, but the meeting may impose conditions or restrictions on the powers listed in s 179 going forward.

fields.reference: Powers exercisable only by Board resolution at a meeting (s 179(3), Meetings Rule 8)
fields.prompt_md: Which powers must the Board exercise by a resolution passed at a Board meeting?
fields.gist_md: Making calls; buy-back under s 68; issuing securities; borrowing; investing funds; loans, guarantees and security; approving the financial statements and Board's report; diversifying the business; approving amalgamation, merger or reconstruction; and taking over a company or buying a controlling or substantial stake. The Rules add political contributions, appointing or removing KMP, and appointing the internal and secretarial auditors.

fields.prompt_md: To whom may the Board delegate its resolution-only powers, and in which companies may it decide by circulation?
fields.gist_md: By a resolution passed at a meeting it may delegate to a committee of directors, the managing director, the manager or another principal officer, or the principal officer of a branch, on conditions it sets. In a Section 8 company some of these matters (borrowing, investing funds, and giving loans or guarantees) may be decided by circulation instead of at a meeting.

fields.reference: Matters needing a special resolution under s 180(1)
fields.prompt_md: Which Board actions require the company's consent by special resolution?
fields.gist_md: Selling, leasing or disposing of the whole or substantially the whole of an undertaking; investing in trust securities the compensation received on a merger; borrowing above the total of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium (temporary bank loans excepted); and remitting or giving time for a director's debt. Every borrowing resolution must state the total amount the Board may borrow.
fields.exceptions_md: The clause on investing merger compensation in trust securities does not apply to a private company.

fields.definition_md: An undertaking is one in which the company's investment exceeds 20% of its net worth in the last audited balance sheet, or which produced 20% of total income in the previous year. 'Substantially the whole' means 20% or more of the undertaking's value in that balance sheet.
Loans repayable on demand or within six months of being made, such as cash credit, bill discounting and seasonal short-term loans, but not loans raised for capital expenditure.

fields.prompt_md: When may shareholders step into functions that normally belong to the Board?
fields.answer_md: In exceptional cases: where a majority of directors act in bad faith, where the Board is incompetent or cannot act (for example every director is interested in a resolution, or no Board can immediately be formed), or where a deadlock or uncertainty over who has the power leaves it with the shareholders.

fields.reference: Applying for a DIN (s 153, Appointment Rule 9)
fields.prompt_md: How is a DIN applied for and by whom is the form verified?
fields.gist_md: A person intending to be a director of an existing company files Form DIR-3 electronically with the prescribed fee, signed by his own digital signature, with photograph, proof of identity, proof of residence and a verified specimen signature. A company secretary in full-time employment, or the MD, a director, CEO or CFO of the company concerned, verifies it digitally. For proposed directors without a DIN in a new company, up to three may be given in the incorporation form INC-32. A person without a surname gives his father's or grandfather's surname with a declaration in DIR-3A.

fields.prompt_md: How long does the Central Government take to allot a DIN, and what happens to a defective application?
fields.gist_md: It decides within one month of receipt. If the application is defective, the applicant is told through the website and email and has 15 days to resubmit. An application still defective, or not corrected in time, is rejected or marked invalid and the fee is neither refunded nor adjusted. A DIN is valid for life and cannot be given to anyone else.

fields.prompt_md: What are the rules on holding a single DIN and on intimating it?
fields.gist_md: No person who already has a DIN may apply for or hold another. An existing director intimates his DIN to every company where he is a director within one month of receiving it, and each company furnishes the DINs of all its directors to the Registrar within 15 days of that intimation. Failure by the company, and each officer in default, brings a fine of ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

fields.prompt_md: Can a company compensate a director for loss of office (s 202)?
fields.answer_md: Only a managing director, whole-time director or manager, not any other director. The amount is capped at the lower of the pay for the rest of his term or three years, calculated on his average pay for the preceding three years. Nothing is payable if he resigns in the ordinary course or on reconstruction and joins the successor, if his office is vacated under s 167(1), or if he was guilty of fraud, breach of trust, gross negligence or mismanagement, or helped bring about his own removal.

fields.prompt_md: When winding up follows a director's departure, is compensation for loss of office still payable?
fields.answer_md: No payment can be made if winding up starts before or within 12 months after he left and the assets, after winding-up costs, cannot return shareholders their capital with premium. It is also barred if the winding up was caused by his negligence or default. Pay for professional or other services rendered separately is not compensation.

fields.prompt_md: If financial statements must be restated because of fraud or non-compliance, whose remuneration is recoverable?
fields.answer_md: That of any past or present managing director, whole-time director, manager or CEO who during the restated period received pay (including stock options) above what the restated numbers would have allowed. The company must recover the excess.

fields.prompt_md: What does s 185 prohibit, and what can a company do for entities in which its directors are interested?
fields.gist_md: A company cannot, directly or indirectly, lend (including through a book debt) to, or guarantee or secure loans of, any director of it or of its holding company, a partner or relative of such a director, or a firm in which such a director or relative is a partner. For a person in which a director is interested, it may lend, guarantee or secure if a special resolution is passed (with an explanatory statement giving full particulars and the purpose) and the borrower uses the money for its principal business. 'Interested' covers a private company where the director is a director or member, a body corporate where he or other directors control 25% or more of the voting power, and a body corporate that acts on the lending company's Board's directions.

fields.prompt_md: In which cases is s 185 not breached?
fields.gist_md: A loan to a managing or whole-time director under service conditions that apply to all employees, or under a scheme the members approved by special resolution. A company that lends or gives guarantees in its ordinary business and charges at least the Government-security yield for the tenor. A holding company's loan to, or guarantee or security for loans of, its wholly owned subsidiary, and its guarantee or security for a bank or institution loan to a subsidiary, provided the subsidiary uses the funds for its principal business.
fields.exceptions_md: A private company is also outside s 185 if no other body corporate has invested in it, its borrowings from banks, institutions or bodies corporate are below the lower of twice its paid-up capital or ₹50 crore, and it is not in default on those borrowings.

fields.prompt_md: What penalty follows a loan made in breach of s 185, and who bears it?
fields.answer_md: The company: ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh. The defaulting director and the person who received the loan, guarantee or security: imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine of ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh, or both. Others who knowingly took part are not covered by this penalty.

fields.prompt_md: When and how must a director disclose his interest?
fields.gist_md: He gives written notice at the first Board meeting at which he takes part, at the first meeting of each financial year, and at the first meeting after any change. This covers every body corporate, firm or association in which he holds shares, a directorship or any other interest. If he is interested in a contract or arrangement, he discloses it at the Board meeting where it is discussed and does not participate. Interest arises where the other party is a body corporate in which he holds more than 2% or is promoter, manager or CEO, or a firm in which he is partner or owner. If he becomes interested after the contract, he discloses forthwith or at the next Board meeting.
fields.exceptions_md: The section does not apply to a contract between two companies where the directors of one hold no more than 2% of the paid-up capital of the other.

fields.prompt_md: What is the effect of a contract entered without s 184 disclosure, or with the interested director taking part?
fields.answer_md: It is voidable at the company's option. The interested director also does not count toward the quorum or vote on that item. Disclosure to the whole Board need not be formal where all directors already know the facts (Ramakrishna Rao v Bangalore Race Club).

fields.case_name: Ramakrishna Rao v Bangalore Race Club
fields.held_md: Where every director already knows the facts of a colleague's interest, a formal disclosure is unnecessary.

fields.definition_md: A director who is directly or indirectly concerned or interested in a contract or arrangement, through himself, a relative, or a firm or body corporate in which he or a relative is partner, director or member. His presence is not counted for the quorum on that item.

fields.prompt_md: How is the Board quorum fixed when interested directors are two-thirds or more of the Board?
fields.answer_md: The quorum is the number of non-interested directors present, and it cannot be fewer than 2.

fields.definition_md: An office held by a director, or by any person, firm, private company or body corporate, that gives the holder anything from the company (salary, fee, commission, perquisites, rent-free accommodation or otherwise) beyond a director's own entitlement.

fields.prompt_md: Which transactions with a related party need the Board's prior approval at a meeting?
fields.gist_md: Sale, purchase or supply of goods or materials; selling, disposing of or buying property; leasing property; availing or rendering services; appointing an agent to buy or sell goods, services or property; the related party's appointment to an office or place of profit in the company, its subsidiary or associate; and underwriting subscription to the company's securities. Above prescribed thresholds, prior approval of the members by resolution is also needed.

fields.reference: Thresholds for member approval of related-party transactions (s 188)
fields.prompt_md: What thresholds trigger a members' resolution for a related-party transaction?
fields.gist_md: Goods: above the lower of 10% of turnover and ₹100 crore. Property sale or purchase: above the lower of 10% of net worth and ₹100 crore. Services: above the lower of 10% of turnover and ₹50 crore. Office or place of profit: monthly remuneration above ₹2.5 lakh. Underwriting commission: above 1% of net worth. Limits are tested on the transaction alone or taken together with earlier transactions in the year.

fields.prompt_md: Who may not vote on a related-party resolution, and when are shareholder approvals not needed?
fields.answer_md: Members who are related parties cannot vote on it, unless 90% of the members are promoters, relatives or related parties. Shareholder approval is not needed for transactions in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis or between a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary. Contracts not ratified are voidable, and the beneficiaries must compensate the company.

fields.reference: Omnibus approval by the Audit Committee (Meetings Rule 6A)
fields.prompt_md: What conditions govern omnibus approval of related-party transactions?
fields.gist_md: The Audit Committee, with Board approval of the criteria, may grant it for repetitive transactions. The criteria fix an annual aggregate ceiling, a per-transaction ceiling, the disclosures needed, review intervals and transactions excluded.
