Each approval names the related parties, the nature and duration, the maximum amount and the price basis. Unforeseen transactions are allowed up to ₹1 crore each. An approval lasts at most one financial year and cannot cover sale or disposal of the company's undertaking.

fields.reference: 2026 revision: SEBI LODR Regulation 23 materiality (2025 amendment)
fields.prompt_md: How did the 2025 amendment to LODR Regulation 23 change the materiality test for related-party transactions?
fields.gist_md: Materiality is now scale-based and tied to the listed entity's annual consolidated turnover, rather than one flat percentage for every company. Recurring operational transactions may be assessed separately. The aim is that large entities get proportionate limits and small transactions do not need shareholder approval.

fields.reference: 2026 revision: subsidiaries and approvals under Regulation 23
fields.prompt_md: What new oversight applies to unlisted subsidiaries' related-party transactions, and how did shareholder approvals change?
fields.gist_md: The listed entity's Audit Committee must approve material related-party transactions of its unlisted subsidiaries, and the parent must monitor subsidiary transactions above the set thresholds and disclose them in consolidated reporting. Greater reliance is placed on Audit Committee omnibus approval, and shareholder approval is needed only when revised materiality limits are exceeded.

fields.prompt_md: 2026 revision: how did Regulation 23 change disclosures and the Audit Committee's role?
fields.answer_md: Disclosures were consolidated into standard electronic templates, removing duplication across quarterly, annual and exchange filings; the entity must keep its financial statements and exchange disclosures consistent. The Audit Committee must review the justification for each transaction, test that it is fair and at arm's length, and record the reasons for approving it.

fields.case_name: Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co v Synthetics & Chemicals Ltd
fields.held_md: A director's disqualifying interest is a personal interest, not an official one; it can be financial and can arise from a fiduciary duty or a close family tie such as husband and wife or father and son.

A director must disclose his interest formally at the Board meeting even when the other directors already know about it, and he may not take a profit from his fiduciary position without the beneficiaries' consent.

fields.prompt_md: How often must a Board meet, and what relaxation exists?
fields.gist_md: The first meeting is within 30 days of incorporation, and then at least four meetings a year with no more than 120 days between two consecutive meetings, unless the Central Government exempts. A One Person Company with more than one director, a small company and a dormant company comply by holding at least one meeting in each half of the calendar year with a gap of at least 90 days.
fields.exceptions_md: The half-yearly relief does not apply to an OPC with only one director. Under SS-1, independent directors must meet at least once a calendar year.

fields.text_md: First Board meeting within {{c1::30 days}} of incorporation; at least {{c2::4}} meetings a year; gap not more than {{c3::120 days}}. For OPC, small and dormant companies, one meeting in each half-year with a gap of at least {{c4::90 days}}.

fields.reference: Participation by video conferencing (s 173(2), Meetings Rule 3)
fields.prompt_md: What must a company ensure when directors join a Board meeting by video or audio-visual means?
fields.gist_md: Arrangements must prevent connection failure and let each participant hear and see the others clearly. The chairperson and the company secretary must safeguard the meeting's integrity with security and identification, check only the intended director is attending, record and minute the proceedings, and keep the recording at least until the audit for that year is complete. The notice states the option and a venue where the recordings will be made. A director who does not intimate his wish to join electronically is presumed to attend in person; he may make one standing declaration at the start of a calendar year, valid for that year.

fields.prompt_md: What is the notice period for a Board meeting, and what if the business is urgent?
fields.gist_md: At least 7 days' written notice to every director at his registered address, whether in India or abroad, by hand, post or electronic means. For urgent business a shorter notice is allowed if at least one independent director (where the company has one) attends. If no independent director attends, the decisions are final only on ratification by at least one independent director, and the notice must say it is short notice. The penalty for failure to give notice is ₹25,000 on each officer responsible.

fields.prompt_md: What does SS-1 require the notice of a Board meeting to contain, and on which days may a meeting not be held?
fields.answer_md: A serial number, day, date, time and full venue address, the electronic participation option with details and a contact for confirming, and the agenda with notes to agenda; each item is numbered, and proof of sending is kept. It is issued by the company secretary or another authorised person, by the means a director has specified. A meeting can be held at any time and place on any day except a national holiday (26 January, 15 August, 2 October and any other the Central Government declares).

fields.prompt_md: How is the Board quorum fixed and what if the Board falls below it?
fields.gist_md: One-third of the total strength or two directors, whichever is higher. Directors joining by video or audio-visual means count. Any fraction is rounded up to one, and vacant seats are left out of the total strength. If vacancies take the number below quorum, the continuing directors may act only to fill vacancies up to the quorum or to call a general meeting. If interested directors are two-thirds or more of the Board, the quorum is the non-interested directors present, at least two.
fields.exceptions_md: Section 174 does not apply to an OPC with a sole director. A Section 8 company's quorum is the lower of eight directors or 25% of its strength, never less than two.

fields.prompt_md: Under SS-1, when must a quorum be present and what is the quorum rule for committees?
fields.answer_md: It must be present throughout the meeting. For a committee, all its members must be present to form a quorum unless the Act, other law, the articles or the Board say otherwise.

fields.prompt_md: What conditions must be met for the Board or a committee to pass a resolution by circulation?
fields.gist_md: The draft and papers must go to all directors or members at their registered addresses by hand, post, courier or prescribed electronic means, and a majority of those entitled to vote must approve it. If at least one-third of the directors require that it be decided at a meeting, the chairperson must put it to a meeting. The resolution is noted at the next Board or committee meeting and made part of its minutes. Under SS-1 directors get at most 7 days from circulation to respond.

fields.prompt_md: Name the major items SS-1 says cannot be passed by circulation.
fields.answer_md: Approving the financial statements and Board's report; borrowing other than by debentures; investing funds; loans, guarantees and security; political contributions; calls on shares; MD, WTD and manager remuneration; appointing or removing KMP; appointing a person as MD or manager in more than one company; filling a director's casual vacancy; buy-back; issue of securities; amalgamation, merger or reconstruction; diversification; takeover or acquiring a substantial stake; related-party sanctions not at arm's length or in the ordinary course; payment for loss of office; and appointing secretarial and internal auditors.

fields.prompt_md: What are the requirements for preparing and keeping minutes?
fields.gist_md: Minutes of every general meeting, class meeting, Board and committee meeting, and postal ballot are recorded in consecutively paged books and signed within 30 days. They give a fair and correct summary of the proceedings, record all appointments, and for Board meetings the directors present and any who dissented or did not concur in each resolution. Draft minutes go to all directors within 15 days. The chairperson may exclude matter that is defamatory, irrelevant or immaterial, or detrimental to the company's interests. Minutes are evidence of the proceedings and raise a presumption the meeting was validly held.

fields.prompt_md: Which Secretarial Standards must a company follow for meetings, and what are the penalties for breaching s 118?
fields.answer_md: SS-1 (Board meetings) and SS-2 (general meetings), issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India. Failure to comply with s 118 for a meeting attracts a penalty of ₹25,000 on the company and ₹5,000 on each officer in default.

fields.reference: Inspection of minutes of general meetings (s 119)
fields.prompt_md: Who may inspect the minutes of general meetings, and for how long each day?
fields.gist_md: Any member, free of charge, in business hours at the registered office, for at least two hours on each business day, subject to reasonable restrictions in the articles or general meeting. The books are kept in electronic form there, and a member gets a copy within 7 days of asking and paying the fee.

fields.text_md: Statutory register forms: investments not in the company's name {{c1::MBP-3}}; loans, guarantees and investments under s 186 {{c2::MBP-2}}; contracts with interested directors {{c3::MBP-4}}; buy-back {{c4::SH-10}}; members {{c5::MGT-1}}; debenture-holders {{c6::MGT-2}}.

fields.prompt_md: Which other statutory records must a company keep besides the member and loan registers?
fields.answer_md: Deposit register; register of charges; foreign register of members and debenture-holders; register of beneficial owners; copies of annual returns; minute books; postal-ballot register; books of account and cost records; register of directors and KMP; register of renewed and duplicate share certificates; and register of sweat equity shares.

fields.prompt_md: Where are registers kept and who may inspect them?
fields.gist_md: At the registered office, or at another place in India where more than one-tenth of the members on the register live, if a special resolution approves it and a copy is given to the Registrar in advance (the resolution is filed in MGT-14). Members, debenture-holders, other security holders and beneficial owners may inspect free during business hours, and anyone else for a fee. Extracts are free; copies cost the prescribed fee.

fields.reference: Board composition under SEBI LODR Regulation 17
fields.prompt_md: What does Regulation 17 require of a listed company's Board?
fields.gist_md: A mix of executive and non-executive directors with at least one woman director and at least half non-executive. If the chairperson is non-executive, at least one-third of the Board must be independent; if the chairperson is executive, at least half must be independent.

fields.reference: Audit Committee: who must have one and its composition (s 177, Meetings Rule 6)
fields.prompt_md: Which companies need an Audit Committee and how is it made up?
fields.gist_md: Every listed company, and every public company with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more, turnover of ₹100 crore or more, or total loans, borrowings, debentures and deposits above ₹50 crore (measured on the last audited accounts). It has at least 3 directors, independent directors forming a majority, and a majority including the chairperson able to read and understand financial statements. The composition is disclosed in the Board's report.
fields.exceptions_md: The independent-majority rule does not apply to a Section 8 company.

fields.prompt_md: What does the Audit Committee's written terms of reference cover?
fields.gist_md: Recommending the appointment, pay and terms of auditors (for a government company only the remuneration, since the CAG appoints); reviewing auditor independence, performance and audit effectiveness; examining the financial statements and auditors' report; approving related-party transactions and any later change (and granting omnibus approval); scrutinising inter-corporate loans and investments; valuing undertakings or assets when needed; evaluating internal financial controls and risk management; and monitoring the use of funds raised in public offers.

fields.prompt_md: What authority does the Audit Committee have, and what right do auditors and KMP have in its meetings?
fields.answer_md: It may investigate any matter within its remit, take outside professional advice and have full access to company records. It may call for the auditors' comments on internal controls, audit scope and the financial statements before they go to the Board, and discuss with internal and statutory auditors and management. Auditors and KMP may be heard when it considers the auditor's report but cannot vote. If the Board rejects a recommendation, the Board's report must say so with reasons.

fields.prompt_md: Which companies need a vigil mechanism and how does it work?
fields.gist_md: Every listed company, every company accepting public deposits, and every company with bank or public financial institution borrowings above ₹50 crore. Directors and employees can report genuine concerns, with safeguards against victimisation and direct access to the Audit Committee chairperson in exceptional cases. The Audit Committee oversees it (a conflicted member steps aside); other companies' Boards nominate a director to play that role. Repeated frivolous complaints may be met with action such as a reprimand. The mechanism is disclosed on the website and in the Board's report.

fields.prompt_md: Under LODR, what limits does a director face on committee memberships and what must the annual report on governance include?
fields.answer_md: A director may not belong to more than 10 committees or chair more than 5, across all companies where he is a director. The annual report has a separate governance section, a management discussion and analysis (opportunities and threats, segment performance, risks, financial against operational performance, and HR or industrial relations developments) and full remuneration details, with an auditor's certificate of compliance sent to the stock exchange.

fields.reference: CSR: who must comply and the spend (s 135)
fields.prompt_md: Which companies must have a CSR Committee and how much must they spend?
fields.gist_md: A company with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more in the preceding financial year. It forms a CSR Committee, frames a CSR policy and spends at least 2% of its average net profit of the last three years. A company that stays below all thresholds for three consecutive years is released until it meets them again.

fields.prompt_md: Who sits on the CSR Committee and what does it do?
fields.gist_md: At least three directors, with at least one independent director. An unlisted public company or a private company that need not have independent directors has none; a private company with two directors has both. For a foreign company it includes the person authorised to receive notices and one other nominee. The committee recommends the CSR policy and changes, recommends projects for Board approval, and sets up a transparent monitoring mechanism.

fields.prompt_md: List the statutory duties of a director.
fields.gist_md: Act in line with the articles; act in good faith to promote the company's objects for the benefit of members as a whole, and in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, the community and the environment; use due and reasonable care, skill and diligence and independent judgment; avoid situations of direct or indirect conflict with the company's interest; not seek undue gain for himself or his relatives, partners or associates; and not assign his office.

fields.case_name: Milan Sen v Guardian Plasticate Ltd
fields.held_md: Whether a company needs fresh capital through a rights issue is for the directors to decide, and the court will not interfere unless there is clear mala fides or breach of trust.

fields.prompt_md: Are directors agents of the shareholders who nominated them?
fields.answer_md: No. They exercise their powers in good faith for the company, not as agents of members, and even the group that nominated a director cannot dictate how he votes. Board powers are co-extensive with the company's, but the shareholders' supremacy ultimately prevails because they appoint the Board.

fields.prompt_md: When can directors become personally liable to outsiders?
fields.answer_md: When they make contracts for the company that are ultra vires or beyond their authority, when they contract in their own name instead of the company's, and when they issue a prospectus that breaks the Act or the SEBI ICDR rules or contains misstatements.

fields.prompt_md: Who may make political contributions and how?
fields.gist_md: A company may contribute any amount to a political party registered under s 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, by a resolution passed at a Board meeting. There is no monetary ceiling. The contribution must be disclosed in the profit and loss account for the year. Payments likely to affect public support for a party, and spending on politically linked publications, count as contributions.
fields.exceptions_md: A Government company and a company that has existed for less than three financial years cannot contribute.

fields.term: Inspection, inquiry and investigation: how they differ
fields.definition_md: Inspection is a routine check that a company obeys the law and is not negative in itself. Inquiry looks into a specific complaint or suspicion. Investigation is the deepest probe, gathering evidence to support prosecution of a suspected violation. Inquiry and investigation need a reason such as information or a complaint.

fields.reference: Registrar's power to call for information (s 206(1)-(3))
fields.prompt_md: How can the Registrar call for information and documents from a company?
fields.gist_md: On scrutiny of filed documents or on information received, he may by written notice require the company to furnish information or explanation, or produce documents, within a reasonable time. Officers must respond to the best of their knowledge, and former officers may be called on for past periods. A second notice requiring books of account and papers for inspection at a stated time and place may follow if there is no reply, the reply is inadequate, or the documents show an unsatisfactory state of affairs; the Registrar records his reasons in writing.

fields.reference: Inquiry by the Registrar and inspection by the Government (s 206(4)-(5))
fields.prompt_md: When may the Registrar hold an inquiry, and what can the Central Government order?
fields.gist_md: If satisfied from information or a representation that the business is run for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in breach of the Act, or that investors' grievances are not addressed, he may inquire after giving the company a written order setting out the allegations and a hearing. The Central Government may direct the Registrar or an Inspector to carry out the inquiry, or order inspection of books by an Inspector or other authority. Where the business was for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, each officer in default is punishable for fraud under s 447.

fields.prompt_md: What must officers do during an inspection, and what powers does the inspecting officer have?
fields.gist_md: Every director, officer and employee must produce documents, give the statements and explanations required and render all assistance. The Registrar or Inspector may copy the books and mark them as inspected, and has the civil-court powers of discovery and production of documents, summoning and examining persons on oath, and inspecting books and registers anywhere. Disobedience brings up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh, and a convicted director or officer is deemed to vacate office and is disqualified from holding office in any company.

fields.prompt_md: When may the Registrar or an inspector search and seize a company's records?
fields.gist_md: When he has reasonable ground to believe that books and papers relating to the company, a director, KMP, auditor or company secretary may be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or hidden. He needs an order from the Special Court to enter, search and seize. The papers must be returned within 180 days of seizure, but may be recalled for a further 180 days by written order. CrPC provisions on search and seizure apply.

fields.prompt_md: To whom does an inspector report and what can the report recommend (s 208)?
fields.answer_md: A report with documents goes to the Central Government, and it may recommend further investigation.

fields.reference: When the Central Government orders an investigation (s 210)
fields.prompt_md: What triggers an investigation into a company's affairs under s 210?
fields.gist_md: A report from the Registrar or Inspector under s 208, a special resolution of the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or public interest. It must order an investigation when a court or the Tribunal orders in any proceeding that the affairs should be investigated.

fields.prompt_md: How does an investigation pass to the SFIO and what follows?
fields.gist_md: The Central Government may assign it on an Inspector's or Registrar's report, a special resolution, public interest, or a request from a Central or State Government department. From then no other agency of the Central or State Government may investigate offences under the Act in that matter and must hand over its records. An Investigating Officer with an Inspector's powers under s 217 conducts it, and the company and its current and former officers must cooperate. The SFIO sends an interim and a final report, and the Central Government may direct it to prosecute.

fields.prompt_md: Who can apply to the Tribunal for an investigation, and on what grounds?
fields.gist_md: At least 100 members or members holding one-tenth of the voting power (for a share-capital company), or one-fifth of the persons on the register (for one without share capital), with supporting evidence; or any other person where the Tribunal sees circumstances suggesting fraud or unlawful purpose or oppression, fraud or misfeasance by those who formed or managed the company, or that members have not been given the information they might reasonably expect. The Tribunal may order the Central Government to appoint inspectors; if the allegations are proved, officers in default are punished for fraud under s 447.

fields.prompt_md: What is the purpose of an investigation into ownership under s 216?
fields.answer_md: The Central Government may appoint inspectors to find the true persons who are or were financially interested in the company's success or failure, who could control or materially influence its policy, or who hold a beneficial interest or are significant beneficial owners of its shares.

fields.prompt_md: What can an inspector require of the company's people, and how long may he hold records?
fields.gist_md: All present and former officers, employees and agents must preserve and produce the books and papers and give assistance. He may keep the records no more than 180 days, extendable by a further 180 days by written order. He has civil-court powers of discovery, summoning and examination on oath, and inspection of documents anywhere. Government, police and statutory authorities must assist him with the Central Government's prior approval, and the Government may agree reciprocal arrangements with foreign states.

fields.reference: Protection of employees during an investigation (s 218)
fields.prompt_md: What must a company do before dismissing or punishing an employee while an investigation is pending?
fields.gist_md: Obtain the Tribunal's approval before discharging, suspending, punishing or worsening the terms of an employee. If the Tribunal does not respond within 30 days of the application, the company may proceed. A party unhappy with the Tribunal's objection may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within 30 days of the notice.

fields.reference: Investigating related bodies and seizing documents (s 219, s 220)
fields.prompt_md: How far can an inspector's reach extend, and when can he seize documents?
fields.gist_md: With the Central Government's prior approval he may investigate a subsidiary or holding company, a subsidiary of its holding company, a company managed by the same managing director or manager, a company whose Board is its nominees or accustomed to follow its directions, and its managing director, manager or employee, so far as relevant. If he has reasonable grounds to fear the records will be destroyed, altered or hidden, he may seize them after letting the company copy them at its cost, and he keeps them only as long as needed up to the end of the investigation.

fields.prompt_md: What restrictions may the Tribunal place on securities during an investigation (s 222)?
fields.answer_md: On a complaint or in connection with a s 216 investigation, where facts about securities cannot be found out otherwise, it may direct that the securities be subject to restrictions for up to 3 years. It may also freeze assets while the investigation proceeds.

fields.reference: Action on the inspector's report and expenses (s 224, s 225)
fields.prompt_md: What may the Central Government do after an inspector's report, and who pays for the investigation?
fields.gist_md: It may prosecute any person found criminally liable, bring proceedings in the company's name to recover damages for fraud or misfeasance or to recover misapplied property, or begin winding up in the public interest, with the company indemnifying it for costs. The Government pays the expenses first but is reimbursed by a convicted person or one ordered to pay damages or restore property (as the court specifies), by the company to the extent of sums it recovers, and if no prosecution follows, by the company, managing director or manager dealt with in the report or, for a s 213 investigation, the applicants, as the Government directs.

fields.definition_md: A settlement of disputed claims by mutual concessions. There must be a dispute, and a scheme under which members give up their rights entirely is not a compromise.

A term of wide meaning that covers reorganising share capital by consolidating or dividing shares of different classes, including altering preferential or special rights, and can be between the company and members or creditors, or classes of them.

fields.case_name: Re Investment Corporation of India Ltd
fields.held_md: Every mode of reorganising share capital, including interfering with preferential and other special rights of shares, can properly form part of an arrangement with members.

fields.definition_md: A process by which two or more companies join to form a new entity, or one or more are absorbed into another so that the transferor loses its existence and its shareholders become shareholders of the transferee. The Act does not define the word.

fields.reference: Who may propose a scheme and what the application carries (s 230(1)-(2))
fields.prompt_md: Who can apply to the Tribunal for a compromise or arrangement, and what must the application show?
fields.gist_md: The company, any creditor or member, or the liquidator may apply, jointly if they wish, and the Tribunal orders meetings of the creditors or members (or their classes). The application discloses all material facts including the latest financial position and auditor's report, pending investigations, any capital reduction, and any corporate debt restructuring scheme agreed by at least 75% of secured creditors in value. A debt restructuring scheme comes with a creditors' responsibility statement, safeguards for other creditors, an auditor's report that post-restructuring funding meets the liquidity test, and a registered valuer's valuation.

fields.reference: Notice of the scheme meeting (s 230(3), Compromise Rules)
fields.prompt_md: What must accompany the notice of a Tribunal-ordered meeting, and where must it be published?
fields.gist_md: A statement giving the details of the scheme, any valuation report, and its effect on creditors, KMP, promoters, non-promoter members, debenture-holders and directors' material interests, in Form CAA-3 style individual notices. It also states pending investigations, directors', KMP and promoters' shareholdings and recent changes, approvals received, and a declaration that the scheme serves non-promoter and minority holders. The notice goes on the company's website and, for listed companies, to SEBI and the stock exchanges and in newspapers.

fields.prompt_md: Who must be sent notice of a scheme, and who can object?
fields.gist_md: The Central Government, income-tax authorities, RBI, SEBI, the Registrar, the stock exchanges, the Official Liquidator, the Competition Commission and any affected sectoral regulator. They must make any representation within 30 days of receipt, failing which they are presumed to have none. Only persons holding at least 10% of the shares or owed at least 5% of total outstanding debt may object to the scheme.

fields.reference: Approval and sanction of a scheme (s 230(6)-(8))
fields.prompt_md: What majority approves a scheme and what follows after sanction?
fields.gist_md: A majority in number representing three-fourths in value of the creditors, or members, of each class present and voting in person, by proxy or postal ballot, and then the Tribunal's sanction. The scheme then binds the company, all creditors and members (or the liquidator and contributories in a winding up). The order must give convertible preference shareholders the choice of arrears of dividend in cash or in equity, protect creditor classes, deal with variation of shareholder rights under s 48, and may include an exit offer for dissenters. The order is filed with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt.

fields.prompt_md: Can the Tribunal dispense with a creditors' meeting?
fields.answer_md: Yes, where creditors, or a class of them, holding at least 90% in value agree and confirm by affidavit to the scheme. Also, a scheme must conform to the accounting standards, confirmed by the company's auditor.

fields.prompt_md: What can a scheme under s 230 include, and what powers does the Tribunal keep after sanction (s 230(11), s 231)?
fields.answer_md: It can include a takeover offer (for a listed company, under the SEBI regulations). After sanction the Tribunal supervises implementation, may modify the scheme or give directions, can require reports on its working, and may order winding up if the scheme cannot be implemented and the company cannot pay its debts under it.

fields.reference: Merger or amalgamation: the Tribunal route (s 232(1)-(2))
fields.prompt_md: What must be circulated for the meeting in a merger or demerger scheme?
fields.gist_md: The draft scheme adopted by the directors of the merging companies, confirmation that a copy was filed with the Registrar, a directors' report on its effect on each class of shareholders, KMP, promoters and non-promoter shareholders (including the exchange ratio and valuation difficulties), the expert's valuation report, and a supplementary accounting statement if the last annual accounts end more than 6 months before the first meeting. The auditor also certifies that the proposed accounting treatment conforms to the accounting standards.

fields.reference: What the Tribunal's merger order may provide (s 232(3))
fields.prompt_md: List the matters a Tribunal's sanction order for a merger may deal with.
fields.gist_md: Transfer of the transferor's undertaking, property and liabilities from a date set by the parties; allotment of shares or debentures by the transferee; continuation of pending legal proceedings; dissolution of the transferor without winding up; provision for dissenters; allotment to non-resident holders per FDI norms; transfer of employees; if a listed transferor merges into an unlisted transferee, the transferee stays unlisted and dissenters are paid out at a predetermined formula or valuation; set-off of fees paid on the transferor's authorised capital against the transferee's; release of charges; and any incidental matters.

fields.prompt_md: When is the merger order filed, when does the scheme take effect, and what continuing reporting applies?
fields.gist_md: A certified copy of the order is filed with the Registrar within 30 days of receipt. The scheme must state an appointed date from which it is deemed effective, not a later date. Until the scheme is complete, each company files a yearly statement certified by a practising chartered accountant, cost accountant or company secretary showing whether the scheme is being complied with as ordered.

fields.definition_md: A company other than a public company whose paid-up share capital does not exceed ₹4 crore (or a higher prescribed amount not above ₹10 crore) and whose turnover does not exceed ₹40 crore (or a higher prescribed amount not above ₹100 crore). Holding companies, subsidiaries, Section 8 companies and companies under special Acts are excluded.

fields.prompt_md: Which companies may use the simplified merger procedure and how does it work?
fields.gist_md: Two or more small companies, a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary, and prescribed classes (including two or more start-ups, or a start-up with a small company). Notice inviting objections goes to the Registrar and Official Liquidator and persons affected, with 30 days to respond. Members holding at least 90% of the total shares approve it, each company files a declaration of solvency with its Registrar, and creditors representing 9/10ths in value approve at a meeting on 21 days' notice or in writing. The transferee files the approved scheme with the Central Government, Registrar and Official Liquidator.

fields.prompt_md: How is a fast-track scheme confirmed, and when can it be sent to the Tribunal?
fields.gist_md: If the Registrar and Official Liquidator raise no objections within 30 days, the Central Government registers the scheme and confirms it. If it thinks the scheme is against the public interest or creditors' interest, it may apply to the Tribunal within 60 days, and the Tribunal may then require the s 232 process or confirm the scheme. Registration dissolves the transferor without winding up.

fields.prompt_md: What are the effects of registering a fast-track merger scheme?
fields.answer_md: Property and liabilities pass to the transferee, charges on the transferor's property continue against the transferee's, pending legal proceedings continue by or against the transferee, unpaid sums for dissenting shareholders or creditors become the transferee's liability, and any shares the transferee held in itself, directly or through a trust or subsidiary, are cancelled.

fields.prompt_md: Can an Indian company merge with a foreign company?
fields.gist_md: Yes, with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India. A foreign company may merge into an Indian company, or the reverse, and the shareholders of the merging company may be paid in cash, depository receipts or partly each. The chapter applies to jurisdictions notified by the Central Government.

fields.prompt_md: How can a transferee acquire the shares of dissenters after a scheme is approved?
fields.gist_md: Where holders of at least nine-tenths in value of the shares involved approve the scheme or contract, the transferee may buy out the dissenting holders through notice to them, with the Tribunal available to dissenters on application. The consideration is deposited in a separate bank account.

fields.prompt_md: How is the minority's exit price fixed in a scheme (Rule 27)?
fields.answer_md: By a registered valuer's valuation, and the company must verify the minority's details within two weeks of receiving the amount of the consideration. The cut-off date for corporate actions benefiting the transferee is announced in advance.

fields.reference: Amalgamation ordered in the public interest (s 237)
fields.prompt_md: When can the Central Government order amalgamation, and how are members and creditors protected?
fields.gist_md: When it is satisfied that it is essential in the public interest, by an order in the Official Gazette, which may also continue pending proceedings against the transferee. Members and creditors keep as nearly as possible the same interest or rights; if they end up with less, they receive compensation assessed by a prescribed authority and published in the Gazette and paid by the transferee. A person aggrieved may appeal to the Tribunal within 30 days of publication of the assessment.

fields.prompt_md: What must a share-transfer offer circular contain under s 238?
fields.answer_md: Prescribed information and a statement by the transferee about the steps taken to ensure cash will be available; it can be circulated only after registration. The Registrar may refuse registration, which can be appealed to the Tribunal.

fields.prompt_md: What is the majority-rule principle and what does the rule in Foss v Harbottle say?
fields.answer_md: Decisions of a duly convened general meeting on matters the company can lawfully deal with bind the minority. Where a wrong is done to the company, the company itself is the proper plaintiff, so an individual member cannot sue the directors for it. The reason is that members agree to be governed by the majority.

fields.held_md: A wrong done to a company can be redressed only by the company, acting through its majority, so one member cannot sue in respect of it.
A resolution of the majority passed at a duly convened meeting, on a matter the company is competent to deal with, binds the minority and the company.
Where the Act or articles need a special majority, a bare majority is not enough, and where wrongdoers control the company, the minority may sue on its behalf.

fields.prompt_md: State the exceptions to the rule in Foss v Harbottle.
fields.answer_md: An individual member may sue where: the act is illegal or ultra vires; the majority commits a fraud on the minority; wrongdoers in control prevent the company from suing; a resolution needing a special majority was passed by a simple majority, or on defective notice; the member's personal rights (to vote, to have his vote recorded, to stand for election, to enforce the articles) are infringed; or directors and the majority breach a duty to the company's detriment.

fields.case_name: Nagappa Chettiar v Madras Race Club
fields.held_md: An individual shareholder may enforce his own rights against the company, such as the right to vote, to have his vote recorded and to stand for election as director.

Minority shareholders were allowed to sue where two directors who controlled the company sold its land to one of them at an undervalue (£4,250) and it was later resold for far more; breach of duty by those in control that benefits them is actionable even without a fraud.
Provisions of the memorandum and articles are mandatory and cannot be waived by a bare majority of members.

fields.definition_md: Not defined in the Act. Courts treat it as conduct that clearly falls short of the fair dealing every investing shareholder can expect, so that the complaining member is made to bear something unjust, harsh or tyrannical.

fields.reference: Who can apply to the Tribunal for relief from oppression (s 244)
fields.prompt_md: What are the eligibility thresholds for applying under s 241?
fields.gist_md: In a company with share capital: at least 100 members or one-tenth of the total number of members, whichever is less, or members holding at least one-tenth of the issued share capital, and the applicants must have paid all calls and other dues on their shares. Without share capital: at least one-fifth of the members. The Tribunal may waive these requirements, and one or more eligible members may apply for all with the written consent of the rest.

fields.case_name: Rajmundhry Electric Corporation v V Nageswar Rao
fields.held_md: If some consenting members later withdraw their consent, the petitioners' right to proceed is not affected: the validity of the petition is judged on the facts at the time it was presented.

fields.prompt_md: On what grounds can a member apply for relief, and can the Government apply?
fields.gist_md: A member may apply if the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the public interest, oppressive to any member, or prejudicial to the company, or if a material change in management or control (Board, manager or ownership) makes prejudicial conduct likely, provided he qualifies under s 244. The Central Government may itself apply where affairs are run against the public interest, as may be done where management is guilty of fraud, misfeasance, persistent negligence or breach of trust, business is not run on sound or prudent principles, or it harms the trade or industry or is meant to defraud creditors or members. All applications go to the Principal Bench.

fields.prompt_md: What orders can the Tribunal make on proving oppression or mismanagement?
fields.gist_md: If it finds the conduct oppressive or prejudicial and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members although just and equitable grounds for it exist, it may make any order to end the matters complained of. That includes regulating future conduct, ordering purchase of shares by members or the company (with reduction of capital), restricting share transfer or allotment, terminating or modifying agreements with the managing director, directors or others, setting aside fraudulent preferences made within three months, removing directors or the managing director, recovering undue gains, appointing directors to report, imposing costs, and interim orders. A certified copy goes to the Registrar within 30 days.

fields.prompt_md: After a Tribunal order under s 242 ends a director's or manager's agreement, what follows (s 243)?
fields.answer_md: No claim for damages or compensation for loss of office lies against the company. The person may not be appointed or act as managing director, other director or manager of that company for five years without the Tribunal's leave, which it grants only after notice to the Central Government. A person who knowingly acts in breach, and any director knowingly party to it, faces a fine of up to ₹5 lakh.

fields.prompt_md: What can members or depositors seek by a class action, and who qualifies?
fields.gist_md: A prescribed number of members or depositors (for example, at least 100 or the prescribed percentage, and for a company without share capital one-fifth of members) may apply on behalf of all if the company's affairs are being conducted prejudicially. The Tribunal may restrain ultra vires acts or breaches of the memorandum or articles, declare void a resolution altering them if passed by suppressing material facts, restrain acting on it or on illegal acts, restrain action contrary to members' resolutions, and award damages or compensation against the company, its directors, the auditor or any expert or adviser for fraudulent, unlawful or misleading acts.
fields.exceptions_md: Section 245 does not apply to a banking company.

fields.prompt_md: How does the Tribunal handle admitted class action applications, and what is the penalty for not complying with its order?
fields.answer_md: Public notice goes to all class members or depositors, similar applications are consolidated into one with a lead applicant chosen by the class (or appointed by the Tribunal), two applications on the same cause are not allowed, and costs are borne by the company or the person responsible. Its order binds the company, all members, depositors, the auditor and any expert or adviser. The company is fined ₹5 lakh to ₹25 lakh, and each officer in default faces up to 3 years' imprisonment and a fine of ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

fields.prompt_md: Which provisions on fraud and damages apply to proceedings under s 241 or s 245 (s 246)?
fields.answer_md: Sections 337 to 341, applying with the necessary changes.

fields.reference: Acts of directors whose appointment is defective (s 176)
fields.prompt_md: Are acts of a director valid if his appointment turns out to be defective?
fields.gist_md: Acts done in good faith by a person as director are not invalid merely because it was later found that his appointment was defective or he was disqualified, or that his appointment had terminated under the Act or articles. This does not extend to acts as managing director after he ceased to hold office, to cases where there was no appointment at all or it was illegal, to acts done after the company learned of the defect, or to acts ultra vires the Act.

fields.case_name: Varkey Souriar v Keraleeya Banking Co Ltd
fields.held_md: Acts done as managing director after he ceased to hold that office are invalid: it was not an irregular exercise of power but the exercise of power by a person with no authority at all.

fields.reference: Squeeze-out of minority by a 90% holder (s 236)
fields.prompt_md: What happens when an acquirer reaches 90% of the equity share capital?
fields.gist_md: He or the group must notify the company of an intention to buy the remaining shares and offer to buy them at a price determined by a registered valuer. The minority may also offer their shares to the majority at that price. If the full purchase is not completed, the section continues to apply to the residual minority. A scheme where the price is set by the promoters and minority holders have no choice whether to tender does not comply.
